The initiative, announced by Mayor Darrell Steinberg during a State of the City event on August 23, 2023, aims to provide an alternative to 9-1-1 for individuals experiencing mental health crises. [2, 3, 5] The new system is designed to connect them with mental and behavioral health services and substance abuse treatment. A key part of this strategy involves Wellspace Health developing a 13-acre wellness campus at 6780 Stockton Boulevard. [2] This campus will host a Crisis Receiving for Behavioral Health Center (CRBH) to serve those with mental health or substance abuse issues. [2] <2> On August 3, 2023, U.S. District Judge Troy L. Nunley issued a temporary restraining order preventing the City of Sacramento from clearing homeless encampments for at least 14 days. This ruling was in response to a motion filed by the Sacramento Homeless Union, which argued that displacing unhoused residents during a period of excessive heat, with forecasted temperatures frequently exceeding 90 degrees, was dangerous and harmful. In his decision, Judge Nunley concurred with the union's assessment of the risks posed by the heat. He ordered both the city and the union to meet and discuss potential solutions to balance the interests of all parties. The order was later extended until August 31, 2023. <3> The New York City Council successfully voted on July 13, 2023, to override Mayor Eric Adams' veto of a significant legislative package aimed at reforming the CityFHEPS rental assistance program. [3, 5] A central component of this package was the codification into law of the elimination of a rule that required unhoused individuals to stay in a shelter for 90 days before qualifying for housing vouchers. [3] The situation was complex, as Mayor Adams had already preemptively eliminated the 90-day rule via an emergency executive action on June 16, 2023, just weeks after the Council initially passed the bills in May and ahead of his formal veto on June 23. [2, 4, 5, 9] The Mayor argued that while he supported ending the 90-day rule, the Council's broader package, which also eased income and work requirements, was too costly for the city. [5, 9] The Council's 42-8 override vote sought to enact the entire reform package into law. [3] <4> The National Coalition for the Homeless hosted its 2023 Leadership Conference on Friday, September 29, and Saturday, September 30, 2023, at the Hilton Capitol Hill in Washington D.C. The event, themed "Unlocking the Potential of Leaders who have Experienced Homelessness," brought together nearly 250 advocates, policymakers, service providers, and individuals with lived experience of homelessness. The two-day gathering focused on networking, storytelling, artwork, and collaboration. A key feature was that all workshop sessions were led by people who have personally experienced homelessness. Special guest speakers included Representative Cori Bush, and the agenda included an awards ceremony on the evening of September 30th. <5> The City of San Diego initiated a 'Safe Sleeping program' to provide a sanctioned, legal camping alternative for individuals experiencing homelessness. Planned for city-owned land, the program offers a secure environment with amenities like tents, restrooms, meals, and connections to supportive services, representing a different option from traditional congregate shelters. On June 28, 2023, Mayor Todd Gloria announced the opening of the first site. This initial location, at the City's Central Operations Yard in Golden Hill (near 20th and B Street), officially opened to clients on June 29, 2023. Operated by the nonprofit Dreams for Change, the site initially had a capacity for 136 tents, each able to accommodate up to two people. <6> Representative Maxine Waters (D-CA) introduced the 'Ending Homelessness Act of 2023' (H.R. 4232) to the House of Representatives on June 21, 2023, as part of a larger legislative package to address the housing crisis. The bill aims to establish a path to end homelessness in the United States through several key provisions. It proposes expanding the Housing Choice Voucher program, making it a federal entitlement to be phased in over eight years, which would guarantee assistance to all qualifying households. The legislation also seeks to legally prohibit housing discrimination based on an individual's source of income or their status as a veteran. Furthermore, the bill allocates significant funding for affordable housing and support services, including $10 billion over five years for the national Housing Trust Fund and McKinney-Vento homeless assistance grants, and provides funds for outreach and case management. <7> In January 2023, New York City's primary shelter system documented its highest census in the 40 years of record-keeping, with over 72,000 people sleeping in shelters each night. [2, 6] This record was published by the Coalition for the Homeless in its "State of the Homeless 2023" report. [2, 6] The report identified the worsening crisis as being exacerbated by the influx of asylum seekers combined with a systemic failure to address the lack of affordable housing in the city. [2, 6]

[1, 5] This collaborative initiative involves state, federal, local, and veteran-serving organizations working together to achieve "functional zero," a federal benchmark where homelessness is rare, brief, and non-recurring. [2, 3, 6] The campaign's strategy is built on key pillars that include prioritizing supportive housing, increasing access to behavioral health services, making capital investments in veteran housing, and improving care coordination. [4, 7] <2> In 2023, Chattanooga, Tennessee, and the surrounding region achieved a significant 49% reduction in homelessness compared to the previous year. [3] This figure, close to the initially claimed half, was reported in early 2024. An earlier report from April 2023, based on the annual Point-in-Time (PIT) count from January, had indicated a 31% decrease in Hamilton County's homeless population, from 1,144 in 2022 to 785 in 2023. [2, 6] The success in reducing homelessness is attributed to a combination of strategic local efforts. Key initiatives included a focus on providing permanent housing, an Eviction Prevention Initiative supported by $1 million in American Rescue Plan funds, and the development of permanent affordable and supportive housing. [3, 4, 12] Collaborative efforts among the city, the Chattanooga Regional Homeless Coalition, and other service providers to target resources to vulnerable populations were also crucial. [3] Despite these gains, officials note ongoing challenges, including a broader housing crisis marked by rising costs and limited housing availability in the city. [3] <3> On February 8, 2024, New York City Mayor Eric Adams launched the 'Affordable Housing Services' (AHS) initiative, a new program designed to create over 1,500 permanent affordable homes for New Yorkers in the shelter system. [2] The initiative enables non-profit partners to purchase or secure long-term leases on buildings, providing housing for individuals and families who hold City Fighting Homelessness and Eviction Prevention Supplement (CityFHEPS) vouchers. [2] This program is a key component of the Adams administration's strategy to address the city's severe housing shortage and create scalable pathways for residents to move from shelters into permanent homes with strong tenant protections. [2] <4> In its 2024 legislative session, which ran from January 8 to March 7, 2024, the Washington state legislature considered several bills to address housing instability and homelessness. [5, 21] Key proposals included a pair of bills, HB 2114 and its companion SB 5961, aimed at improving housing stability by limiting rent and fee increases to 7% and requiring longer notice periods for such increases. [3, 6] While HB 2114 passed the House, it ultimately died in a Senate committee, and SB 5961 also failed to advance out of its committee. [2, 7, 10] Another legislative effort focused on increasing affordable housing options by authorizing co-living or single-room occupancy housing. [4] While its Senate bill (SB 5901) died, the House version, HB 1998, successfully passed the legislature, [14, 16, 24] <5> On January 9, 2024, Oregon's Governor, Tina Kotek, signed Executive Order 24-02, extending the state of emergency to continue addressing the homelessness crisis. [2, 3, 5, 6] The order directs state agencies to persist in their efforts to reduce unsheltered homelessness, rehouse individuals, and prevent households from becoming homeless, thereby maintaining the response infrastructure established under the initial emergency declaration (Executive Order 23-02) from January 2023. [2, 5, 10] Following the initial declaration, the state reported exceeding its goals; according to Oregon Housing and Community Services, it created 1,032 new low-barrier shelter beds against a goal of 600, rehoused 1,293 families, and prevented 8,886 households from experiencing homelessness. [3, 6] <6> The U.S. Departments of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and Veterans Affairs (VA) announced that homelessness among veterans increased by 7.4% between 2022 and 2023. Data from the 2023 Point-in-Time (PIT) count, an annual census of the homeless population, revealed that 35,574 veterans were experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2023. This represents an increase of over 2,400 individuals from the previous year. A deeper analysis showed that while the number of sheltered veterans grew by 2.6% to 20,067, the number of unsheltered veterans rose by a more significant 14.3% to 15,507. The increase has been attributed by some to the end of pandemic-era housing protections and a broader crisis in housing affordability. <7> On December 15, 2023, the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness (USICH) released a statement from Director Jeff Olivet summarizing the federal government's significant actions in 2023 to address the nation's homelessness crisis. The summary detailed progress made toward the goals of 'All In: The Federal Strategic Plan to Prevent and End Homelessness,' which aims to reduce homelessness by 25% by 2025. Key achievements highlighted include launching the ALL INside initiative to tackle unsheltered homelessness, investing nearly half a billion dollars for unsheltered and rural homelessness, and helping over 424,000 households avoid or exit homelessness through HUD programs. The actual, more detailed USICH Annual Report for Fiscal Year 2023 was formally submitted to the President later, on January 31, 2024. <8> The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD) 2023 Point-in-Time (PIT) count, released on December 15, 2023, identified New York City as having the largest number of individuals experiencing homelessness, with a total of 88,025. This figure represents a significant increase of 39% from 2022 and surpassed Los Angeles, which had 71,320 individuals. The data, gathered on a single night in January 2023, indicates that the overall number of people experiencing homelessness in the U.S. reached over 653,000, a 12% rise from the previous year. State officials attribute the sharp increase in New York to several factors, including the termination of the COVID-19 eviction moratorium, high costs of housing, an influx of asylum seekers needing emergency shelter, and more accurate counting methodologies. <9> The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) released its 2023 Annual Homeless Assessment Report (AHAR) Part 1, which found that on a single night in January 2023, approximately 653,100 people were experiencing homelessness in the United States. This represents a 12% increase, or about 70,650 more people, compared to 2022 and is the highest number recorded since data collection began in 2007. The report, officially released on December 15, 2023, indicated that the increase in homelessness was observed across all population groups, a departure from previous years where increases were driven by a single demographic. Of those experiencing homelessness, 60% were in sheltered locations, while 40% were in unsheltered places not meant for human habitation. This funding, part of a larger $3.16 billion national allocation, marks an 11.5% increase for Maryland over the previous fiscal year. The funds are designated to support housing and various services for individuals experiencing homelessness. Notably, a portion of the funding is specifically allocated for projects aimed at assisting survivors of domestic violence. The state's 10 Continuum of Care organizations will distribute the $68,928,914 to provide these critical services. <2> On April 18, 2024, California Governor Gavin Newsom announced approximately $192 million in Encampment Resolution Fund (ERF) grants to support 20 projects across 17 communities. The funding, administered by the California Interagency Council on Homelessness (Cal ICH), is designated to help transition nearly 3,600 people from encampments into housing. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On June 28, 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court delivered a 6-3 decision in the case of City of Grants Pass v. Johnson, overturning a lower court's ruling. [2, 3, 4] The judgment grants cities expanded authority to enforce ordinances that prohibit homeless individuals from camping in public spaces by using items like blankets or pillows for sleeping. [2, 3] The majority opinion concluded that these local laws do not constitute "cruel and unusual punishment" under the Eighth Amendment, reversing a lower court's finding that had protected individuals when no alternative shelter is available. [2, 3, 4] This decision effectively overturns six years of legal protections established by the 9th Circuit's precedent in Martin v. City of Boise. [2] <2> In a 6-3 decision, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in the case of City of Grants Pass v. Johnson that local ordinances prohibiting homeless individuals from sleeping on public land with items such as blankets, pillows, or cardboard boxes do not violate the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment. [1, 2] The majority opinion held that these laws regulate the conduct of camping on public property, which applies to everyone, rather than punishing an individual's status of being homeless. [1, 2] This landmark ruling gives local governments significantly more latitude to enforce anti-camping laws, a decision with effects expected to extend far beyond the Oregon city at the center of the case. [1, 2] Critics, such as the ACLU, argue that the decision effectively grants cities the authority to jail or fine people for the basic human need to sleep and will lead to increased harassment and criminalization of the unsheltered population. [2] <3> On June 28, 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in the case of City of Grants Pass v. Johnson, reversing a decision by the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. [1, 2, 3] The Court's majority opinion, written by Justice Gorsuch, held that enforcing generally applicable laws regulating camping on public property does not violate the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on "cruel and unusual punishment." [2, 4] This ruling permits cities to enforce such bans against individuals experiencing homelessness, even if there is no available shelter space. [4] The majority opinion was joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Thomas, Alito, Kavanaugh, and Barrett. [3] Justice Sotomayor wrote the dissenting opinion, which was joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson. [3] <4> On May 16, 2024, the Biden administration, through the National Park Service, and the administration of Washington D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser, cleared several homeless encampments in the Foggy Bottom area of the city. [2] The action displaced a number of individuals estimated to be between 60 and 90. [2, 5] The eviction was initially scheduled to begin on May 15 but was partially postponed due to weather. [4] In a statement released on May 17, 2024, critics including the National Homelessness Law Center and other advocacy groups argued that the eviction violated the federal government's own strategic plan to end homelessness by failing to connect the displaced individuals with stable housing options. [5] The groups stated that dozens of tents and personal belongings were discarded and that none of the individuals were moved into stable housing as a result of the clearing. [5] <5> On April 29, 2024, Maryland's Governor Wes Moore announced that the state will receive nearly $69 million in federal funding from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's (HUD) Continuum of Care program. This funding, part of a larger $3.16 billion national allocation, marks an 11.5% increase for Maryland over the previous fiscal year. The funds are designated to support housing and various services for individuals experiencing homelessness. Notably, a portion of the funding is specifically allocated for projects aimed at assisting survivors of domestic violence. The state's 10 Continuum of Care organizations will distribute the $68,928,914 to provide these critical services. <6> On April 18, 2024, California Governor Gavin Newsom announced approximately $192 million in Encampment Resolution Fund (ERF) grants to support 20 projects across 17 communities. The funding, administered by the California Interagency Council on Homelessness (Cal ICH), is designated to help transition nearly 3,600 people from encampments into housing. Of those individuals, around 2,200 are expected to receive permanent housing. This initiative emphasizes providing person-centered services and support to ensure long-term stability for unsheltered individuals. The announcement also included new accountability measures to increase oversight of how state homelessness funding is used by local jurisdictions. <7> On April 17, 2024, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) announced the availability of $12,746,450 in competitive funding for Public Housing Agencies (PHAs) through its Foster Youth to Independence (FYI) Initiative. [2] The funds are designated to provide housing assistance to young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 who have left the foster care system or will be leaving within 90 days, and are currently experiencing or are at risk of homelessness. [1, 6] This funding, provided through Housing Choice Vouchers (HCV), requires PHAs to partner with Public Child Welfare Agencies (PCWAs) to connect these young people with stable housing. [1, 3] The application deadline for PHAs was set for June 17, 2024. [3, 5] The initiative is part of a broader federal effort to prevent and end youth homelessness and help youth on a path to self-sufficiency. [1] <8> In her 2024 State of the City address, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass announced a new initiative, LA4LA, calling on the city's wealthiest residents, corporations, and philanthropic organizations to contribute to a capital campaign. [1, 2] This effort, as outlined by the mayor, aims to use these private funds to acquire more properties for housing the homeless, thereby lowering capital costs and speeding up the process. [1, 2]

metadata.original_text: This time series records homelessness data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2025-06-08 to 2025-08-24. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A report from the Maricopa Association of Governments, released in May 2025, indicated a 28% increase in the unsheltered homeless population in Maricopa County, Arizona, based on a count conducted on January 28, 2025. The total number of individuals experiencing homelessness was 9,734, a 3% rise from the previous year. Officials attributed the spike in the unsheltered population to the expiration of federal pandemic-era funding, which had previously supported over 1,000 shelter beds in the region. A "Safe Outdoor Space" facility was already in operation as of November 2023. The May 2025 report does note that individuals staying at the Safe Outdoor Space are included in the unsheltered count per federal guidelines. <2> Data released by the San Diego County Regional Task Force on Homelessness on May 20, 2025, showed a 7% decrease in the region's homeless population over the past year. [1] The findings originated from the January 2025 Point-in-Time (PIT) Count, an annual census that represents a minimum number of people experiencing homelessness on a single day. [1] The 2025 count, conducted by over 1,700 volunteers, found 9,905 people experiencing homelessness countywide, down from 10,605 in the prior year. [1] The data also highlighted a 14% drop within the city of San Diego. [1] <3> A national survey commissioned by the National Alliance to End Homelessness and conducted by Morning Consult has revealed significant public concern regarding homelessness and housing affordability. [2] The poll, conducted in April 2025, found that 69% of Americans are worried about their ability to maintain stable housing, and 79% are concerned for others in their community. [1] A strong majority, 78%, recognize the connection between their local housing market and the broader economy. [1] The findings highlight a widespread belief that homelessness is primarily an economic issue, with 74% of adults stating that the current economic climate is making housing less affordable. [2] Furthermore, 72% of respondents believe that more affordable housing options would alleviate homelessness in their communities. [2] The survey also indicated that half of all U.S. adults have observed an increase in homelessness in their communities over the past year, with 69% attributing this rise to increasing housing costs. [2] <4> In May 2025, the Trump administration released its fiscal year (FY) 2026 budget proposal, which included significant cuts to the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). An initial 'skinny' budget was released on May 2, with the full, detailed proposal submitted on May 30. The proposal called for a $532 million cut to HUD's Homeless Assistance Grants (HAG) by consolidating the Continuum of Care (CoC) and Housing Opportunities for Persons with AIDS (HOPWA) programs into the Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG) program. In response, housing advocates issued warnings about a potential funding crisis. The National Alliance to End Homelessness projected that the cuts could end funding for over 166,000 permanent supportive housing units, potentially causing more than 218,000 people, many with disabilities and formerly chronically homeless, to lose their housing. The National Low Income Housing Coalition (NLIHC) and Senate Appropriations Vice Chair Patty Murray also voiced strong opposition, stating the cuts would 'eviscerate' HUD funding and increase the risk of homelessness for many families. <5> The City of Chicago, under the leadership of Mayor Brandon Johnson and the Mayor’s Office of Homelessness headed by Chief Homelessness Officer Sendy Soto, has initiated a public engagement survey to inform its new Five-Year Plan on Homelessness. [1, 2] This initiative seeks to foster a co-governance approach by actively involving residents, community stakeholders, and particularly individuals with lived experience of homelessness, in shaping a comprehensive strategy to prevent and end homelessness. [1, 2, 3] The city's framework for this engagement is encapsulated in the acronym ACCTion, standing for Awareness, Curiosity, Connection, and Transformation, aiming to raise awareness and gather meaningful input for the plan's development. [1, 3] <6> According to the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Housing & Homelessness Dashboard, there were 2,415 individuals experiencing homelessness in the county as of April 30, 2025. [2] This represents a 12% decrease, or 316 fewer people, compared to April 2024. [2] The data, which is compiled from the Homeless Management Information System, includes individuals in emergency shelters, transitional housing, and street outreach programs. [2] In April 2025, there was a notable 25% decrease in the number of individuals entering the homeless services system. [2] During that month, 566 people entered the system while 674 exited, resulting in a net decrease in the total number of people experiencing homelessness. [2] While there were overall decreases, the number of unaccompanied youth and veterans experiencing homelessness saw slight increases between March and April 2025. [2] <7> On April 10, 2025, the 'Housing for All Act of 2025' (S.1477) was introduced in the U.S. Senate by Senator Alex Padilla. [1, 2, 3] A press release announcing the bill's reintroduction was issued on April 21, 2025, by Senator Padilla along with Representatives Ted Lieu and Salud Carbajal. [4] The legislation aims to provide a comprehensive approach to the national affordable housing and homelessness crises. [4] It proposes significant federal funding for established programs, including the National Housing Trust Fund, the emergency solutions grant program, and the Continuum of Care program, as well as for innovative local solutions. [4, 6] <8> On March 25, 2025, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a $908 million funding package for homeless services for the 2025-26 fiscal year. [4, 6, 7] This initial approval included funds from the new Measure A sales tax, unspent Measure H funds, and state homeless assistance grants. [4] Subsequently, on April 15, 2025, the Board of Supervisors approved a motion that further detailed the allocation of these funds, specifying which homeless service programs would continue to be funded, at what levels, and which programs would face funding reductions to balance the budget. [5, 6] This second vote resulted in the elimination of $5 million for a landlord engagement program and a $3.9 million reduction to the Department of Health Services' shelter budget, among other adjustments. [5]

[2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] It also allows or requires recipients of federal funding for homelessness assistance to collect health-related data from program participants and share that information with law enforcement where permitted by law. [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] Furthermore, the executive order signals an end to federal support for 'housing-first' policies, instead prioritizing treatment, recovery, and self-sufficiency. [2, 3, 4, 5, 7] <2> On July 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order titled 'Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets,' also referred to as Executive Order 14321. The stated purpose is to address homelessness and increase public safety by redirecting federal resources away from 'Housing First' and 'harm reduction' policies. Instead, the order prioritizes federal grants for states and localities that enforce bans on urban camping and loitering, increase the use of law enforcement, and utilize civil commitment to move individuals into long-term institutional settings for treatment. The order directs the Attorney General, in consultation with the Department of Health and Human Services, to seek the reversal of judicial precedents that may impede the use of involuntary commitment for individuals deemed a risk to themselves or the public. Additionally, it requires the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to increase mandates that recipients of federal homelessness aid with substance use disorders or serious mental illness must participate in treatment services as a condition of receiving assistance. This order moves away from the 'Housing First' model, which has been a bipartisan approach for decades, to a new strategy prioritizing public safety, behavioral health treatment, and the institutionalization of unhoused individuals. Key provisions of the order direct federal agencies to end support for 'Housing First' policies, which provide housing without preconditions like sobriety. Instead, federal grants will be prioritized for jurisdictions that enforce bans on urban camping, loitering, and squatting. The order also makes federal housing assistance conditional on participation in treatment for substance use or mental illness. Furthermore, it encourages the expansion of involuntary civil commitment to move individuals from the streets into long-term institutional settings for treatment, directing the Attorney General to seek the reversal of judicial precedents that impede this policy. [1] The deadline for CoCs to submit this data via the HDX 2.0 portal was set for June 13, 2025, at 8:00 PM EDT. [1] This submission process is for the data collected during the annual PIT count, which is a count of sheltered and unsheltered individuals experiencing homelessness on a single night, typically conducted within the last ten days of January. [7, 8] For 2025, HUD did not change the data collection requirements from the previous year. [4, 8] CoCs were provided with technical guidance and resources to assist with the data submission process. Officials attributed the spike in the unsheltered population to the expiration of federal pandemic-era funding, which had previously supported over 1,000 shelter beds in the region. [1] The 2025 count, conducted by over 1,700 volunteers, found 9,905 people experiencing homelessness countywide, down from 10,605 in the prior year. [1] A strong majority, 78%, recognize the connection between their local housing market and the broader economy. [1] The findings highlight a widespread belief that homelessness is primarily an economic issue, with 74% of adults stating that the current economic climate is making housing less affordable. [2] Furthermore, 72% of respondents believe that more affordable housing options would alleviate homelessness in their communities. [1, 2] This initiative seeks to foster a co-governance approach by actively involving residents, community stakeholders, and particularly individuals with lived experience of homelessness, in shaping a comprehensive strategy to prevent and end homelessness. [1, 2, 3] The city's framework for this engagement is encapsulated in the acronym ACCTion, standing for Awareness, Curiosity, Connection, and Transformation, aiming to raise awareness and gather meaningful input for the plan's development. [2] This represents a 12% decrease, or 316 fewer people, compared to April 2024. [2] The data, which is compiled from the Homeless Management Information System, includes individuals in emergency shelters, transitional housing, and street outreach programs. [2] In April 2025, there was a notable 25% decrease in the number of individuals entering the homeless services system. [2] During that month, 566 people entered the system while 674 exited, resulting in a net decrease in the total number of people experiencing homelessness. [2] While there were overall decreases, the number of unaccompanied youth and veterans experiencing homelessness saw slight increases between March and April 2025. [2]

Prediction target period: from 2025-11-23 to 2026-02-08. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On November 13, 2025, the Trump Administration's Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) released the Fiscal Year 2025 Continuum of Care (CoC) Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO). The notice proposed a strict limit, capping the amount communities can spend on permanent housing at 30%. This significant policy shift places an estimated 170,000 stably housed individuals who rely on CoC assistance at risk of returning to homelessness. <2> Governor Kevin Stitt's 'Operation SAFE' (Swift Action for Families Everywhere) is an initiative to clear homeless encampments from state-owned property in Oklahoma, including underpasses, highways, and other state-controlled land. [2, 3] The operation began in Tulsa, where the governor's office announced its launch on September 4, 2025. [3] The stated goal was to restore order and safety, with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol (OHP) and Department of Transportation (ODOT) leading the efforts. [2, 3] Under the initiative, individuals in encampments on state land are offered a choice: transport to a treatment or housing facility, or arrest and prosecution if they refuse assistance and continue to break the law. [2, 3, 5] The first phase in Tulsa concluded after 14 days, during which 64 sites were cleared and nearly 2 million pounds of debris were removed. [8] Following requests from city leaders, the operation expanded to Oklahoma City, with cleanup efforts beginning on October 27, 2025. [9, 11] In Oklahoma City, the state partnered with the 'Key to Home' program to connect individuals with services and housing. [9] The initiative has been met with criticism, with some service providers and officials arguing that it displaces people without addressing the root causes of homelessness, especially given that shelters are often at or over capacity. [6, 7] There is a national discussion around civil commitment spurred by a presidential executive order: President Trump issued an order in July 2025 titled "Ending Crime and Disorder on America's Streets," which encourages the use of civil commitment for homeless individuals with mental illness or addiction. [14, 15, 20] <3> The city of Sioux Falls, South Dakota, is implementing new measures to support its unhoused community. On August 19, 2025, the City Council passed a new ordinance with a 7-1 vote to prohibit the erection of dwellings, such as tents and shelters, in public places for more than two hours. City officials have emphasized that the ordinance is a tool to connect individuals with services rather than to criminalize homelessness. Before a citation is issued, a city representative must make a documented effort to connect the individual with a community service provider. In addition to this ordinance, the city, in collaboration with Minnehaha County and non-profit partners, has developed a "Community Extreme Weather Plan" for the winter. This plan, announced in October 2025, establishes a leveled response for opening emergency shelter space and coordinating outreach when temperatures become dangerous. <4> A collaborative housing initiative in Benton County, Oregon, has successfully moved 54 households, which includes 122 individuals, from homelessness into stable housing. This achievement surpassed the program's initial goal of housing 51 households by June 30, 2025. The Flexible Housing Subsidy Pool Program, which began in July 2024, was financed with state funds following Governor Tina Kotek's 2023 emergency declaration on homelessness. The initiative is a joint effort between Benton County, the City of Corvallis, and the Community Services Consortium. Key partners in this coordinated response include Unity Shelter, Community Outreach Inc., Vina Moses, and the Corvallis School District. <5> A reentry housing assessment presented in July 2024 to the North Carolina Joint Reentry Council revealed that over a quarter of individuals (28%, or 5,610 people) released from state prisons in the past year were identified as homeless. The assessment defined homelessness as having no verified home plan, self-reporting as homeless, providing an intersection as an address, or being released to a shelter or temporary housing. This issue is a key focus of the state's 'Reentry 2030' initiative, a collaboration with the Council of State Governments aimed at improving outcomes for those leaving prison. The initiative's strategic plan includes a goal to reduce homelessness among this population by 10% annually. The findings were presented amid a broader, statewide 19% increase in homelessness in 2024. In response, North Carolina has been developing a strategic plan to enhance support services, including housing, for the approximately 18,000 people who are released from its prisons each year. <6> In response to a significant, unexpected cut in federal funding, the Chester County government and its employees have launched a month-long drive to donate funds, food, and other necessities to the Chester County Food Bank. The food bank, which serves over 40,000 residents, was faced with a potential loss of up to $1 million in food supplies for the year after the U.S. Department of Agriculture canceled a $250,000 food order. To address the immediate shortfall, the Chester County Commissioners also approved the accelerated release of a $75,000 grant, which is the remaining portion of the Food Bank's allocation from the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA). The county's support for the food bank also includes an ongoing partnership to donate fresh produce grown at the Chester County Prison Work Release Center and the Chester County Youth Center. <7> The Colorado Springs Housing Authority (CSHA) suspended its Housing Choice Voucher program, formerly known as Section 8, after receiving a directive from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) that federal funding would not be provided. [3] This decision placed 2,978 applicants, who had entered the housing lottery held from July 15-17, 2025, on a waitlist with no timeline for when new vouchers would be issued. [3] An applicant was reportedly informed of the suspension on July 16, 2025. [3] While earlier reports in 2025 indicated that the program was paused as early as February, the definitive suspension affecting the new lottery applicants occurred in July. [2, 4] The CSHA confirmed on its website that the HUD directive to pause issuing new vouchers remains in effect. [5] The suspension does not affect individuals who are currently housed through the voucher program. [3, 4] <8> The 'Ending Homelessness Act of 2025,' designated as H.R. 4872, was introduced in the U.S. House of Representatives on August 5, 2025. The bill, sponsored by Rep. Maxine Waters, was referred to the Committees on Financial Services and the Judiciary. The primary goals of the legislation are to address homelessness through several key initiatives. It aims to significantly expand the Housing Choice Voucher program by allocating 500,000 incremental vouchers in fiscal year 2025 and an additional 500,000 each year from 2026 through 2028. The bill seeks to establish an entitlement program for these vouchers, ensuring that all eligible families receive assistance. Furthermore, it proposes the repeal of certain criteria that currently render individuals ineligible for housing assistance and introduces a prohibition on housing discrimination based on the applicant's source of income. <9> SchoolHouse Connection released its second-quarter report for 2025, titled 'State Policy on Child and Youth Homelessness: 2025 Q2 Update,' on July 30, 2025. The update highlights legislative advancements aimed at supporting homeless children and youth. Key progress includes Connecticut's SB 1, which identifies students experiencing homelessness as at risk of chronic absenteeism, and Maine's LD 408, allowing unaccompanied minors to obtain vital records at no cost. The report also notes progress in Illinois with HB 3377 and discusses broader efforts to support homeless students in higher education. <10> On July 29, 2025, the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs unanimously passed the bipartisan Renewing Opportunity in the American Dream (ROAD) to Housing Act of 2025. This marks the committee's first significant bipartisan housing markup in over a decade. The comprehensive legislation, sponsored by Chairman Tim Scott (R-S.C.) and Ranking Member Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), aims to address the nation's housing crisis by increasing housing supply, improving affordability, and enhancing oversight of federal programs. The act incorporates provisions from at least 27 previously introduced bills and includes reforms related to disaster recovery, housing in rural areas and Opportunity Zones, and programs for veterans. Key elements focus on streamlining regulations to remove barriers to new construction, promoting innovative methods like modular housing, and modernizing financing options. The bill also requires the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness to provide annual progress updates to Congress.
